title: Alternation
summary: The | operator, its surprisingly low precedence, why the first alternative that fits wins (not the longest), and grouping alternatives with (?:...).

steps.title: | means or, and it binds loosest
body: `GET|POST` matches `GET` or `POST`. The catch: `|` has the **lowest precedence** of anything in a pattern. It
splits the whole pattern (or the whole group it sits in) into alternatives.
| `^GET\|POST` | `(?:^GET)\|(?:POST)`: GET at the start, or POST **anywhere** |
Put the alternatives in a group to limit them: `^(?:GET|POST) ` is GET or POST, at the start, then a space.
Below, the second line matches although it does not start with a method. Change the pattern to `^(?:GET|POST)`.

steps.prompt: Which pattern means the same as `^cat|dog$`?
steps.explain: `|` splits the whole pattern in two: `^cat` or `dog$`. So `catalog` and `hotdog` both match. `^(?:cat|dog)$` is almost always what was meant.

steps.title: Lines that start with a serious level
prompt: Find log lines that **start** with the level `ERROR`, `WARN` or `FATAL` as a whole word. A level later in the
line does not count, and `WARNING` is a different word (it has its own rule elsewhere).
hints: Group the three levels so the `^` applies to all of them.
steps.explain: Without the group, `^ERROR|WARN|FATAL` finds `WARN` and `FATAL` anywhere. Without `\b`, `WARN` matches the start of `WARNING`.

steps.title: The first alternative that fits wins
body: The engine tries the alternatives **left to right**, at each position, and takes the first one that leads to a
match. It does not look for the longest. So `in|int` on `int count` matches `in`: the first alternative fit.
- **Longer first**: `int|in`. Simple, but fragile when the list grows (`WARN|WARNING` is the same bug).
- **Say where it ends**: `\b(?:in|int)\b`. Now `in` fails at the `\b`, the engine backtracks and tries `int`.
This is the behaviour of .NET, JavaScript, Python, Java, PCRE and Rust (and so rg). POSIX tools are the
exception: `grep -E` and `sed -E` pick the **longest** alternative, so `echo int | grep -oE 'in|int'` prints `int`.
A pattern can behave differently in your C# and in the shell script that checks the same logs.
Turn on the step debugger and watch `in` win before `int` is ever tried.

steps.explain: The first alternative that fits wins. In the third line `in` fits, but then `\b` fails before the `t`, so the engine backtracks into the group and tries `int`.

steps.title: Symptom: WARNING lines tagged as WARN
prompt: **Symptom.** The log tagger extracts the level with the pattern below. On the dashboard, every `WARNING` line is
tagged `WARN`, and the message column starts with `ING:`. It also tags the word `FOREWARNED` in a user's comment.
Fix the pattern so it finds `WARNING` and `WARN` as whole words, the long one in full.
hints: `WARN` is tried first and fits the start of `WARNING`. What if the engine had to see a word end?
steps.explain: The short alternative wins inside the long word. Word boundaries fix both bugs at once, and then the order of the alternatives no longer changes the result. `\bWARN(?:ING)?\b` says the same thing more compactly.

steps.prompt: Complete the check: is this file name an image? The extension must be the last thing in the name, in any case.
steps.explain: `(?:jpe?g|png|gif)` keeps the `|` inside the group, and `$` after the group applies to all three. Without the group, `\.jpe?g|png|gif$` would accept `png.exe`.

steps.title: Durations with their units
prompt: Extract every duration from a log line: a number followed by the unit `ms`, `s`, `m` or `h`, with the whole unit.
`1500ms` must come out as `1500ms`, not `1500m`, and `5 minutes` or `10mb` are not durations.
hints: Try `[0-9]+(?:m|ms|s|h)` and look at what it gives for `1500ms`.
steps.explain: With `\b` after the group, `m` fails inside `ms` or `mb`, and the engine moves on to the next alternative or gives up. Listing the longer unit first is good practice too, but the boundary is what makes it correct.

steps.title: Normalise the log level
prompt: Two services spell levels differently. Write `string? LevelOf(string line)` that finds the **first** whole word
that is one of `WARNING`, `WARN`, `ERROR`, `ERR` or `INFO`, and returns it normalised: `WARNING` becomes `WARN`,
`ERR` becomes `ERROR`, the others stay. Return `null` when there is none.
Use one `Regex` with alternation in a group. `System.Text.RegularExpressions` is already imported.
template: Dojo.Eq("WARNING becomes WARN", "WARN", LevelOf("09:12 WARNING disk 80%"));
Dojo.Eq("WARN stays WARN", "WARN", LevelOf("09:12 WARN retry"));
Dojo.Eq("ERR becomes ERROR", "ERROR", LevelOf("09:13 ERR timeout"));
Dojo.Eq("ERROR stays ERROR", "ERROR", LevelOf("09:13 ERROR timeout"));
Dojo.Eq("the first level word wins", "INFO", LevelOf("09:14 INFO recovered from ERROR"));
Dojo.Eq("INFORMATION and ERRORS are not levels", (string?)null, LevelOf("09:15 INFORMATION ERRORS=0"));
hints: Put the alternatives in a group between two `\b`: `\b(WARNING|WARN|ERROR|ERR|INFO)\b`.
After the match, map the value with a `switch` expression: `"WARNING" => "WARN"`, `"ERR" => "ERROR"`, otherwise the value itself.
